lead: A cycloconverter changes an AC supply of one frequency into an AC output of another frequency without a DC link. It connects the load to the supply through two phase-controlled converter groups, one for each output half cycle. By slowly changing the firing angle of the conducting group, the average output follows a sine of the wanted frequency. This is used for low-speed, high-torque drives such as cement kilns, rolling mills and ship propulsion, where an ordinary inverter-fed motor would need a large gearbox.
prereq: You need the average output of a phase-controlled bridge (Unit 2) and firing-angle control (Chapter 5.1).

blocks.text: The power circuit has two identical phase-controlled bridges connected in antiparallel between supply and load. Call them the P group and the N group. The P group passes current in one direction and gives a positive average voltage; the N group passes current in the opposite direction and gives a negative average voltage. In the common non-circulating mode, only one group conducts at a time.

For the positive output half, the P group is fired. For the negative half, the N group is fired. For a single-phase bridge group, V_d = (2 V_m/π) cos α, where V_m is the peak supply voltage. A three-phase bridge group gives V_d = (3 V_ml/π) cos α, where V_ml is the peak line-to-line supply voltage. Here α is measured from the supply zero crossing where V_d is largest. A large α gives small V_d; a small α gives large V_d.

A sine output comes from changing α during the output half cycle. The wanted output is v_o(t) = V_om sin(2π f_o t), where V_om is its peak and f_o is the output frequency. The control sets cos α proportional to sin(2π f_o t). The bridge then produces short pieces of supply-frequency voltage whose local average follows the sine. The load inductance removes most of the supply-frequency ripple.
The figure shows a 50 Hz supply and a 25 Hz output. The P group conducts for 20 ms, then the N group for 20 ms. One output cycle is 40 ms, so f_o = 25 Hz. The output is a staircase, not a pure sine.

This 1:2 ratio is drawn only to show group changeover; the output is coarse, at two supply half cycles per output half cycle, and is outside the f_o ≤ f_s/3 quality limit. For a smooth staircase use f_o = f_s/3, e.g. 16.7 Hz from 50 Hz.

sections.h3: Firing control and the step-down limit

blocks.text: The firing angle cannot jump instantly. A practical control uses cosine-wave crossing. A cosine wave at supply frequency is compared with a slowly varying reference proportional to the wanted output. The firing pulse is given when the reference crosses the cosine wave.

blocks.where: α is the firing angle in radians; for a single-phase group k = π V_om/(2 V_m) is the voltage ratio and k ≤ 1; ω_o = 2π f_o is the output angular frequency in rad/s; t is time in s.

blocks.text: This method keeps the average output proportional to the reference and reduces harmonic distortion. Two connection modes exist. In circulating-current mode, both groups receive firing pulses all the time. Their instantaneous voltages differ, so current circulates between them. An intergroup reactor limits this current. The reactor adds loss and cost, but the output current is continuous and the change from P to N is smooth. In non-circulating mode, only the group that must conduct is gated; the other is held blocked. The control waits until load current falls to zero before releasing the other group. A small dead time is needed. This mode is cheaper and more efficient but gives a rougher waveform at light load.

Step-down means f_o < f_s, where f_s is the supply frequency. The output is built from a limited number of supply half cycles. If f_o is too close to f_s, each output half cycle contains only one or two supply half cycles, and the staircase is a poor sine. A practical quality limit is f_o ≤ f_s/3. For a 50 Hz supply, the useful output goes up to about 16.7 Hz. Above this limit the output has large low-order harmonics and the motor torque pulsates.

For an RL load, current lags voltage. At large α and light inductance, current may become discontinuous. The average output then no longer follows the simple cosine formula, and the control must compensate. The input displacement factor is close to cos α, so low output voltage means poor input power factor.

Step-up means f_o > f_s. The output must change faster than the supply can naturally commutate the thyristors. Natural commutation fails because the supply voltage does not reverse at the needed time. Step-up cycloconverters therefore need forced commutation, or turn-off devices such as GTOs or IGBTs. The waveform is poor: the output contains subharmonics, that is, frequencies below f_o, and switching loss is higher. Step-up cycloconverters are rarely used in new designs.

Load inductance affects changeover between groups. In non-circulating mode, the control waits for zero current. If current is discontinuous, output voltage rises toward the peak supply voltage during the gap, so the waveform is distorted. In circulating-current mode, the intergroup reactor keeps current continuous, but it wastes power.

The input displacement factor varies through the output cycle. Near the output peak, α is small and the displacement factor is good. Near the zero crossing, α is near 90° and the displacement factor is poor. The supply current also contains harmonics at multiples of f_s and sidebands around them.

Cycloconverters suit low-speed, high-torque drives: cement kilns, rolling mills, ship propulsion and mine hoists. These loads run at a few hertz to about one third of supply frequency and need large torque at low speed. A cycloconverter can feed a synchronous or induction motor directly at that frequency, without a DC link. For higher speeds and ordinary pumps or fans, a DC-link inverter (Unit 4) is smaller and cheaper.

figure.caption: A 50 Hz supply gives a 25 Hz output: the P group conducts for 20 ms, then the N group for 20 ms. The output period is 40 ms.

spec.aria: A timeline shows the positive converter group conducting for 20 milliseconds and then the negative group for the next 20, giving one 40 millisecond output cycle at 25 hertz from a 50 hertz supply.

examples.question: A single-phase step-down cycloconverter feeds an R = 10 Ω, L = 20 mH load from a 230 V, 50 Hz supply. The maximum fundamental output of a single-phase group is 2V_m/π peak = 0.637 V_s = about 146 V RMS for a 230 V supply. Use V_o = 140 V RMS at 12.5 Hz. Find the frequency ratio, the output period, the load reactance, the load impedance, the load current and the power. Check that the frequency ratio is inside the usual 1/3 limit.
steps: Load reactance X_L = 2π f_o L = 2π × 12.5 × 0.020 = 1.571 Ω.
Limit check: 0.25 ≤ 1/3 = 0.333, so the frequency ratio is inside the limit.
examples.answer: The maximum fundamental output is about 146 V RMS. With V_o = 140 V RMS, the frequency ratio is 0.25, the output period is 80 ms, the current is about 13.8 A and the power is about 1.9 kW; the ratio is inside the 1/3 limit.
examples.check:
import math
f_s = 50.0
f_o = 12.5
R = 10.0
L = 20e-3
V = 140.0
ratio = f_o / f_s
T_ms = 1000.0 / f_o
X = 2.0 * math.pi * f_o * L
Z = math.sqrt(R * R + X * X)
I = V / Z
P_kW = I * I * R / 1000.0
print(round(ratio, 2))
print(round(T_ms, 1))
print(round(X, 3))
print(round(Z, 2))
print(round(I, 1))
print(round(P_kW, 1))

traps: Do not draw a DC link or smoothing capacitor inside a cycloconverter. The two converter groups connect the supply straight to the load.
Do not claim that any output frequency can be produced with good quality. Step-down quality needs f_o ≤ f_s/3; above that the staircase is too coarse.
A cycloconverter is not an AC voltage controller. An AC voltage controller keeps f_o = f_s and changes only the RMS value.
Step-up operation (f_o > f_s) is not natural commutation. It needs forced commutation or turn-off devices, and its waveform has subharmonics.
In non-circulating mode the outgoing group must be blocked until load current reaches zero. Ignoring this dead time gives a short circuit between groups.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a cycloconverter and an AC voltage controller?
quiz.a: A cycloconverter changes the output frequency. An AC voltage controller keeps the same frequency and changes only the RMS voltage.

quiz.q: Why are two converter groups needed in a single-phase cycloconverter?
quiz.a: The load current must reverse every output half cycle. One group supplies positive current and voltage; the other supplies negative current and voltage.

quiz.q: A 50 Hz supply feeds a step-down cycloconverter. What is the highest output frequency for good waveform quality? Give the period.
Why does circulating-current mode give smoother output but lower efficiency?
quiz.a: Both groups stay gated, so load current is continuous and changeover is smooth. The intergroup reactor carries a circulating current and wastes power as heat.

quiz.q: In the worked example, if L rises from 20 mH to 40 mH, find the new current and power. Use R = 10 Ω, V_o = 140 V, f_o = 12.5 Hz.
Why does the input displacement factor become poor near the zero crossing of the output voltage?
quiz.a: Near zero output the firing angle is near 90°. The input current lags the supply voltage by a large angle, so cos α is small and the displacement factor is poor.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern drives usually replace cycloconverters with back-to-back voltage-source inverters or matrix converters (Chapter 5.6), because they use smaller filters and give better input current. Research on solid-state transformers and medium-voltage drives still studies direct AC-AC conversion. Cycloconverters remain in very large low-speed synchronous motor drives, such as ore mills and ship propulsion. Search for cycloconverter circulating-current mode, cosine-wave crossing control and subharmonic cycloconverter to go deeper.
